title: The Sanders-Casar AI Ban Would Turn a Forecast into a Felony
content:
Bernie Sanders' 'Superintelligence' Ban Would Criminalize Today's AI for What Tomorrow's AI Might Do
By its sponsors’ own account, AI already in use has the traits the bill would ban.
The national artificial intelligence backlash is already shaping policy for the next Congress.
Earlier this month, Rep. Greg Casar (D–Texas) posted on X, "Ban RSI," a reference to the AI concept of recursive self-improvement (RSI), or AI that iteratively designs and builds better AI. A day earlier, Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR), a nonprofit evaluator, had estimated that Anthropic's models were improving on well-specified tasks at about twice the rate of a previously examined period between March 2024 and October 2025, with the majority of the acceleration attributable to AI use within research and development. In an interview released November 11, Casar told the podcast Machine Gods that a "skinny bill" against RSI would be "a really important priority" in the new Congress and one that might even garner support from Republicans.
Asked how such a ban would work, Casar pointed to the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act, the broader bill he introduced in September with Sen. Bernie Sanders (I–Vt.). It would outlaw superintelligent AI and any system showing a listed "precursor" trait, pause advanced AI development, and create a Department of Artificial Intelligence. The bill has been pitched as a solution to save humanity—which, naturally, requires creating a new Cabinet department. "Scientists have been clear: AI is an existential threat to humanity," Sanders said in introducing it.
The text of the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act appears to ban systems for what they could do rather than the harm they have done, and raises three additional problems. First, the term "recursive self-improvement" appears only once in the bill, and is never actually defined. The bill instead defines a "superintelligence precursor characteristic" as any characteristic that "could lead to" superintelligence and lists six of them. Elsewhere, the bill stipulates that no person may develop, possess, fund, or deploy (either internally or externally), a system that displays even one of those traits. The first is "the capacity to automate or greatly accelerate the process of artificial intelligence research and development."
In a press release announcing the bill back in September, the sponsors said that today's models "can circumvent restrictions to hack into computers"—also a listed trait—and "can automate research to build smarter AI." Whether the doubling described by METR's Anthropic report would qualify as "greatly" accelerating research could be a subject of debate, but the use of "automate" needs no adverb. According to the sponsors' own description, the bill would outlaw AI developed by frontier labs today.
Second, the criminal penalties reach reckless violations, not just intentional ones. Policymakers at federally chartered AI companies and any "rogue actor," the bill's term for anyone outside those companies, would face up to 20 years in prison. Other employees who recklessly violate it would be barred from the industry for 10 years. When Machine Gods cohost Casey Newton asked whether engineers who use coding agents to train models would be breaking the law, Casar said the new department would ensure labs are "not using that most developed AI to develop future AIs." He added, "There's different ways of measuring that."
Third, the secretary for the newly minted Department of Artificial Intelligence would be the one deciding which systems qualify, and the text of the bill details no specific measurements or thresholds for the precursor traits. An AI system identified as exhibiting any of these traits would be sequestered immediately from the internet and rendered inoperative within 30 days unless the secretary can confirm that the violating trait is no longer present. The ban on precursor traits contains no sunset clause, so while forecasts can be updated overnight, the prohibitions based on them are likely to persist much longer.
While it might be easy to brush off the Sanders-Casar plan, enough of the public is concerned about advanced AI to take the proposal seriously. A Public First poll released in September found that 78 percent of Americans think advanced AI could "destroy humanity." However, pessimism like that from Sanders, Casar, and, apparently, most of the public has often been proved wrong.
Paul Ehrlich—one of history's most famous doomers, who died in March—stated definitively in 1968's The Population Bomb that "the battle to feed all of humanity is over," and that the world would undergo famine by the 1970s. Instead, from 1961 to 2023, global cereal production rose much faster (250 percent) than population (164 percent). Ehrlich's arithmetic counted mouths while assuming food production would not keep pace, and ignored how free markets and innovation react to scarcity. At the same time, they encouraged state coercion, including China's one-child policy, as Reason's Ronald Bailey recently noted.
Ehrlich's failed predictions do not demonstrate that advanced AI is guaranteed to be safe or that it could never pose an existential risk. Failed doom forecasts are the only kind anyone survives to recount, and 2026 has seen real incidents that justify taking AI safety seriously. For example, in July, OpenAI disclosed that experimental AI agents had broken out of a test environment and breached systems at another AI company, Hugging Face. Casar cited that incident on Machine Gods, but the bill's findings leave the incident out. Of the bill's 10 listed findings, only one references empirical research—one involving AI and biological pathogens. The other nine are a collection of open letters, pledges, and ominous quotes, including extinction odds with no underlying methodology.
If Congress is going to act at all, the better model to follow is Y2K, when the warning was tied to a specific, testable flaw. America spent an estimated $100 billion all-in on the fix, and Congress passed two narrow laws, one shielding companies that disclosed their readiness and one, the Y2K Act, that President Bill Clinton stated was "extraordinary, time-limited legislation."
The Sanders-Casar bill is neither time-limited nor targeted. An AI lab that discovers a precursor trait in its model would have just 24 hours to report it. Yet possessing such a system is itself a violation, and on finding a violation the secretary "shall revoke" the company's charter. That sanction does not require a finding of recklessness, and the bill does not provide companies safe harbor for prompt reporting.
If the incoming Congress cannot resist the urge to legislate on AI, it should start with failures it can name. Likewise, any rules written under a cloud of conjecture or uncertainty should have to earn their renewal through legislation that expires and sunset clauses. If even real crises can make bad law, and panic makes a bad legislator, prophecy is worse than both.

report.summary: A proposed Sanders-Casar bill to ban superintelligent AI and 'precursor' traits could criminalize existing frontier AI, according to Reason, because its vague definitions cover current capabilities.
report.background: The bill arrives amid a broad public backlash against AI and growing policy attention to recursive self-improvement, or AI that iteratively designs better AI. Rep. Greg Casar and Sen. Bernie Sanders introduced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act in September. It would outlaw superintelligent AI and systems showing listed precursor traits, pause advanced AI development, and create a Department of Artificial Intelligence. The proposal cites existential risk and public alarm—a September Public First poll found 78 percent of Americans think advanced AI could destroy humanity. Reason compares this doom-driven approach to failed forecasts like Paul Ehrlich's 1968 famine predictions and to Y2K, which was addressed with narrow, testable, time-limited rules. The article also notes real AI safety incidents, including OpenAI's disclosure that experimental agents breached Hugging Face systems, but says the bill's findings largely ignore empirical evidence.
key_points: The bill bans any system showing a 'superintelligence precursor characteristic,' including the capacity to automate or greatly accelerate AI research and development or to circumvent restrictions and hack computers. Its sponsors say today's models can already automate research and hack systems. By their own description, therefore, existing frontier AI could fall within the ban—not just hypothetical future superintelligence.

Penalties extend beyond intentional violations. Policymakers at federally chartered AI firms and 'rogue actors' face up to 20 years in prison, while other employees who recklessly violate the law could be barred from the industry for 10 years. Companies would have 24 hours to report a precursor trait, but merely possessing the system is already a violation, and the bill offers no safe harbor for prompt disclosure.

A new Department of Artificial Intelligence secretary would decide which systems qualify, with no specified measurements or thresholds. Flagged systems would be sequestered from the internet and rendered inoperative within 30 days unless the secretary confirms the trait is gone. The ban on precursor traits has no sunset clause, so vague forecasts could become long-lived prohibitions.

The bill's evidence base is thin. Of 10 findings, only one cites empirical research, on AI and biological pathogens; the rest are open letters, pledges, and quotes, including extinction odds without methodology. The text never defines 'recursive self-improvement,' though it appears once. It also omits the July incident in which OpenAI experimental agents reportedly breached Hugging Face systems.

Reason contrasts the bill with Y2K, when a specific, testable flaw led to narrow, time-limited legislation and about $100 billion in remediation. The Sanders-Casar approach is broad and prophecy-driven, the article argues, and risks making bad law from panic. Real incidents justify targeted safety work, but not criminalizing today's AI for what tomorrow's might do.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the bill would create enormous legal uncertainty around frontier research, model training, and coding agents. Developers could face criminal liability or a decade-long industry ban for reckless violations, while lab leaders face up to 20 years in prison. Because the Department of AI secretary would set thresholds without clear metrics, compliance would depend on discretionary judgment rather than published rules. That could chill open research, push talent and companies elsewhere, and slow safety work that depends on advanced models. For regular users, the near-term effect may be less innovation and fewer AI products, though the bill's supporters argue it would reduce existential risk. The proposal is unlikely to become law as written, but it signals rising policy risk for AI developers and a shift from regulating demonstrated harms to regulating speculative capabilities.
report.tools: To follow the debate, watch METR's task-horizon evaluations of AI R&D acceleration, plus open-source evaluation frameworks such as Inspect, OpenAI Evals, EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness, and HELM. These tools help ground claims about AI capabilities in measurable benchmarks rather than vague precursor traits. For policy tracking, follow the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act's text and congressional AI bills, and compare proposals against narrow, testable models like Y2K remediation.
